summary: The Vergecast episode is mostly an interview with Wired's Kate Knibbs about Mike Smith, who pleaded guilty to AI music streaming fraud. He generated hundreds of thousands of AI songs and used bots to stream them, and was ordered to repay about $8.09M. The discussion covers AI slop on streaming platforms, enforcement and platform incentives. The episode opens with a 90-second news roundup that includes two relevant items: preorders for Apple's $299 Home View smart display, and JPMorgan Chase blocking AI agents from doing banking tasks for customers. The rest is ads.
speakers_or_authors: David Pierce (host, The Verge); Kate Knibbs (Wired)
relevance_reason: The main interview is about AI music fraud and slop, not about how people interact with computers. Only the short news segment touches the themes: the agents-versus-websites fight (JPMorgan blocking agents) and Apple's always-listening home display.
themes: Agents versus websites that block them
Always-listening home devices and reactions to them

claims.claim: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said the bank is blocking AI agents from doing banking tasks on customers' behalf, which the host frames as part of a wider fight between agents and the websites and apps they want to access.
claims.quote: JP Morgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon just said that the company is blocking agents from doing banking things on customers behalf.

claims.claim: Apple's $299 Home View smart display is up for pre-order and is designed as a central control system for the family's smart home and communications.
claims.quote: Apple's $299 smart display is up for pre-order now and it's designed to be kind of your family's central control system.

claims.claim: Much of the early reaction to Apple's Home View is people saying they don't want another screen or another always-listening device to manage.
claims.quote: they just simply do not want another screen, another device, another thing to manage and worry about and have listening all the time.

claims.claim: Smith used an AI song generator, fake artists and bot networks to stream the songs on loops. The government ordered him to repay $8,091,843.64.
claims.quote: number was $8,091,843.64 was what the government ordered him to repay

claims.claim: Streaming platforms generally do not prohibit AI music. Spotify recently removed 75 million AI-generated songs, and the prohibited conduct was artificial stream inflation.
claims.quote: Spotify just removed 75 million AI generated songs but there's nothing disallowing AI like broadly speaking

claims.claim: Knibbs expects most online content to become at least AI-assisted, and thinks a clean AI versus not-AI label will become infeasible for platforms to maintain.
claims.quote: I don't think it's feasible to come up with a like this is AI this is not AI like two categories

commercial_interest: The episode carries sponsor reads (AWS AI, Jira/Atlassian, Outshift by Cisco, Rippling AI, Schwab, Apple Watch). None are tied to the guest or the main story. The Apple Home View item is a news mention, not a sponsorship.
older_event: The main story is the Mike Smith case, which began with his arrest in 2024 and is now at the sentencing stage, so it mostly covers events older than 30 days. The new items are the Home View pre-orders and the JPMorgan agent-blocking comment, both dated Oct 14, 2026.
